Does Economic Growth Translate into Longer Lives?

An Interactive Analysis of GDP per Capita and Life Expectancy, 2000–2024

Data Visualization
Plotly
Economic Development
Public Health
World Bank
Published

October 26, 2026

Introduction

Economic growth is often viewed as a major driver of improvements in living standards. Higher incomes can help households afford better nutrition, healthcare, and housing, while governments may gain additional resources to invest in public health infrastructure.

However, economic prosperity does not necessarily translate into longer lives at the same rate everywhere. Economies with similar income levels may have very different health outcomes, and some lower-income economies have achieved substantial improvements in life expectancy without comparable economic growth.

This motivates the central research question:

How is GDP per capita associated with life expectancy, and how has this relationship evolved across economies and regions between 2000 and 2024?

To investigate this question, I use World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI) data to construct an interactive Plotly bubble chart. The visualization allows readers to examine the relationship between economic development and longevity across economies, regions, and years.

I complement the visualization with correlation analysis, a log-linear regression, regional comparisons, and an analysis of changes in GDP per capita and life expectancy between 2000 and 2024.

The goal is to identify meaningful patterns and exceptions rather than establish a causal relationship between income and health.

Data and Methods

Data Source

The analysis uses the World Bank’s World Development Indicators database, covering 2000–2024.

Three indicators are included:

Variable Indicator Code Description
GDP per capita NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD GDP per capita, PPP, constant international dollars
Life expectancy SP.DYN.LE00.IN Life expectancy at birth, total population
Population SP.POP.TOTL Total population

GDP per capita is measured using purchasing power parity (PPP), which accounts for differences in price levels across economies.

Life expectancy at birth represents the expected number of years a newborn would live if prevailing mortality patterns remained unchanged.

Population determines bubble size in the visualization.

Data Cleaning

The original dataset contained 6,650 observations across 266 World Bank entities and 25 years.

After removing aggregate groups and observations with missing or invalid values, the cleaned dataset contains:

  • 4,916 economy-year observations
  • 199 economies
  • 25 years (2000–2024)
  • 7 geographic regions

The cleaned data form an unbalanced panel because not every economy has valid observations in every year.

Visualization Design

The interactive chart uses four visual dimensions:

Visual Element Variable Purpose
X-axis GDP per capita, PPP Economic development
Y-axis Life expectancy Population health
Bubble size Population Relative population scale
Bubble color Geographic region Regional comparison
Animation Year Changes over time

GDP per capita is displayed on a logarithmic scale because income levels vary considerably across economies.

The logarithmic scale makes it easier to compare lower-income economies while preserving the full range of the income distribution.

The interactive animation allows readers to explore how individual economies move over time.

Interactive Visualization

The following chart allows readers to explore the relationship between income and life expectancy across economies and over time.

How to interact with the chart:

  1. Hover over a bubble to view the economy, year, GDP per capita, life expectancy, and population.
  2. Click the Play button to animate changes from 2000 to 2024.
  3. Drag the year slider to examine a specific year.
  4. Click a region in the legend to show or hide its economies.

Figure 1. Interactive relationship between GDP per capita and life expectancy, 2000–2024. Bubble size represents population, and color represents geographic region. Source: World Bank WDI.

The chart is rendered directly from data/wdi_clean.csv as an interactive Plotly widget in this page.

Key Findings

1. Higher GDP per Capita Is Associated with Longer Life Expectancy

The interactive visualization reveals a strong positive relationship between GDP per capita and life expectancy.

Across the full dataset, the Pearson correlation between GDP per capita and life expectancy is:

\[ r = 0.673 \]

When GDP per capita is transformed using the natural logarithm, the correlation increases to:

\[ r = 0.825 \]

This suggests that the log-income specification describes the observed relationship more closely than the untransformed income measure.

To quantify the relationship, I estimate a pooled log-linear regression:

\[ LifeExpectancy_{it} = \alpha + \beta\ln(GDPpc_{it}) + \varepsilon_{it} \]

where:

  • \(i\) represents an economy.
  • \(t\) represents a year.
  • \(LifeExpectancy_{it}\) is life expectancy at birth.
  • \(GDPpc_{it}\) is GDP per capita, PPP.
  • \(\varepsilon_{it}\) represents unexplained variation.

The estimated regression is:

\[ \widehat{LifeExpectancy}_{it} = 12.867 + 6.093\ln(GDPpc_{it}) \]

The estimated coefficient on log GDP per capita is positive, and the regression has an R-squared of approximately 0.681.

This implies that a 1% increase in GDP per capita is associated with approximately 0.061 additional years of predicted life expectancy.

A doubling of GDP per capita corresponds to:

\[ 6.093 \times \ln(2) \approx 4.22 \]

or approximately 4.22 additional years of predicted life expectancy.

Importantly, these estimates describe an association rather than a causal effect.

The regression also pools repeated observations from the same economies. Therefore, conventional standard errors may not fully account for dependence across observations.

2. Substantial Regional Differences Remain

The positive global relationship masks important regional differences.

The following table summarizes average life expectancy across economy-year observations:

Region Average Life Expectancy
North America 79.69 years
Europe & Central Asia 76.53 years
Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 73.94 years
Latin America & Caribbean 73.19 years
East Asia & Pacific 71.41 years
South Asia 70.63 years
Sub-Saharan Africa 59.25 years

North America and Europe & Central Asia have relatively high average life expectancies, while Sub-Saharan Africa has substantially lower average longevity.

The gap between North America and Sub-Saharan Africa is approximately:

\[ 79.69 - 59.25 = 20.44 \text{ years} \]

These regional differences suggest that economic development is not the only factor associated with population health.

Differences in healthcare systems, infectious disease burdens, education, infrastructure, and institutional conditions may contribute to the observed variation.

However, the present analysis does not directly estimate the contribution of these factors.

These averages are unweighted across available economy-year observations and should not be interpreted as population-weighted regional life expectancy.

3. Life Expectancy Increased Over Time, but Progress Was Not Continuous

The annual analysis indicates that average life expectancy increased substantially between 2000 and 2024.

Across available economies, average life expectancy increased from approximately 67.02 years in 2000 to 73.66 years in 2024.

However, the number of economies with complete observations varies across years.

To address this limitation, I construct a balanced endpoint comparison using only the 189 economies with complete observations in both 2000 and 2024.

Indicator 2000 2024
Mean GDP per capita, PPP $18,756.75 $27,003.36
Mean life expectancy 66.94 years 73.55 years

Within these same 189 economies, average GDP per capita increased by approximately 44.0%, while average life expectancy increased by 6.61 years.

This comparison reduces the influence of changing sample composition between the two endpoints.

Nevertheless, the observed improvements cannot establish that income growth caused longer life expectancy.

The time series also reveals a temporary reversal around the COVID-19 pandemic.

Average life expectancy decreased from approximately 72.72 years in 2019 to 71.47 years in 2021, before recovering to approximately 73.66 years in 2024.

This pattern highlights that improvements in population health are not necessarily continuous.

4. Economic Growth and Longevity Do Not Always Move Together

A particularly interesting finding emerges when comparing individual economies between 2000 and 2024.

Economy GDP per Capita Change Life Expectancy Change
Malawi +31.9% +21.39 years
Rwanda +215.1% +20.22 years
Zimbabwe −15.5% +17.03 years
Burundi +1.7% +16.20 years

Rwanda experienced substantial improvements in both economic output per person and life expectancy.

However, Zimbabwe experienced a decline in measured GDP per capita while life expectancy increased by approximately 17 years.

Similarly, Burundi experienced only modest measured income growth but recorded a substantial increase in life expectancy.

These examples demonstrate that improvements in population health do not always correspond to comparable changes in GDP per capita.

They also illustrate why individual economy trajectories are important for interpreting the global income–health relationship.

Deeper Economic Interpretation

Why Might Income and Life Expectancy Have a Nonlinear Relationship?

The association between income and life expectancy may be stronger at lower income levels than at higher income levels.

At relatively low income levels, additional economic resources may improve access to basic necessities such as clean water, nutrition, sanitation, and essential healthcare.

These improvements may produce substantial gains in population health.

At higher income levels, many basic needs may already be met, and further increases in income may be associated with smaller improvements in longevity.

This provides a possible economic explanation for why a logarithmic income scale is useful.

However, the log-linear regression alone does not establish a causal diminishing-returns mechanism.

Why Doesn’t GDP per Capita Fully Explain Longevity?

GDP per capita measures average economic output rather than the distribution or effectiveness of resources.

Two economies with similar GDP per capita may differ in healthcare accessibility, educational attainment, disease prevalence, income inequality, and public policy.

Consequently, similar income levels do not necessarily imply similar health outcomes.

Furthermore, the relationship between income and health may operate in both directions.

Higher incomes may support better health, while healthier populations may contribute to economic productivity.

This potential reverse causality makes it difficult to interpret the observed relationship as a direct causal effect.

What Do Country-Level Exceptions Tell Us?

Country-level exceptions provide an important qualification to the overall positive relationship.

The examples of Zimbabwe and Burundi show that substantial improvements in life expectancy can occur even when measured income growth is limited or negative over the study period.

These observations suggest that health outcomes may be influenced by factors not captured by GDP per capita alone.

Potential explanations include public health improvements, disease prevention, and changes in healthcare accessibility.

These remain hypotheses rather than conclusions directly tested by the current analysis.

The interactive visualization makes such exceptions easier to identify and compare.

Limitations

This analysis has several limitations.

First, correlation does not imply causation. The findings establish statistical associations but do not identify the causal effect of economic growth on life expectancy.

Second, the data form an unbalanced panel. Not every economy has complete observations across the full study period.

Third, the pooled regression combines between-economy and within-economy variation. Conventional standard errors do not account for potential dependence among repeated observations from the same economy.

Fourth, regional and yearly averages are not population-weighted. Each available economy-year observation receives equal weight within its group.

Fifth, the regression does not control for other determinants of health, such as education, healthcare access, inequality, and institutional quality.

Finally, endpoint comparisons do not capture all changes occurring between 2000 and 2024. Individual economies may experience substantial fluctuations within the study period.

These limitations mean that the findings should be interpreted as descriptive evidence rather than causal estimates.

Conclusion

Does economic growth translate into longer lives?

The analysis reveals a strong positive association between GDP per capita and life expectancy across 199 economies from 2000 to 2024.

The correlation between log GDP per capita and life expectancy is approximately 0.825, while the pooled log-linear regression explains approximately 68.1% of the observed variation in life expectancy.

The balanced comparison of 189 economies also reveals substantial long-term improvements in both GDP per capita and life expectancy.

However, significant regional differences remain, and individual economy trajectories demonstrate that improvements in longevity do not always correspond to similar increases in income.

The central takeaway is that economic prosperity is closely associated with population health, but GDP per capita alone cannot fully explain differences in longevity.

For policymakers and researchers, this suggests that economic indicators should be considered alongside direct measures of health and human development.

The interactive visualization provides a way to explore these patterns rather than relying solely on summary statistics.

Reproducibility and Code

The project separates raw data, cleaned data, analysis scripts, interactive visualizations, and statistical outputs.

The repository follows this structure:

Blog7/
├── code/
│   ├── 01_load_data.R
│   ├── 02_clean_data.R
│   ├── 03_plotly_visualization.R
│   └── 04_economic_analysis.R
├── data-raw/
│   └── wdi_raw.csv
├── data/
│   └── wdi_clean.csv
├── results/
│   ├── figures/
│   │   └── gdp_life_interactive.html
│   └── tables/
│       ├── data_quality.csv
│       ├── year_coverage.csv
│       ├── overall_summary.csv
│       ├── regional_summary.csv
│       ├── overall_correlation.csv
│       ├── regression_results.csv
│       ├── regional_comparison.csv
│       ├── yearly_analysis.csv
│       ├── economy_changes.csv
│       └── balanced_comparison.csv
├── index.qmd
└── README.md

To reproduce the analysis, download the complete project and open the Blog7/ folder as the working directory in RStudio.

Install the required R packages:

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",
  "WDI",
  "plotly",
  "htmlwidgets",
  "htmltools"
))

Run the scripts in numerical order:

source("code/01_load_data.R")
source("code/02_clean_data.R")
source("code/03_plotly_visualization.R")
source("code/04_economic_analysis.R")

The cleaned dataset is stored in data/wdi_clean.csv, the interactive visualization is saved in results/figures/, and statistical summaries are exported to results/tables/.

The accompanying README.md provides additional setup instructions and details about the project structure.
